note: Finds that even strong models cannot predict what their own generated code will do, a limitation worth citing in any audit of AI-assisted development.
title: Program Synthesis with Large Language Models
explain_beginner: The paper tested AI systems that can write text on writing short Python programs from plain English requests. It used two sets of tasks, one for beginners and one with harder math word problems. Bigger models solved more tasks, and the best solved about six in ten beginner tasks without extra training. Training on examples helped further. However, even the best models usually could not say what a program would output for a given input. This matters because AI can help write code, but people still need to check whether the code actually behaves correctly.
explain_business: The paper shows that AI systems can turn plain English into short Python programs, and that larger models perform better. Fine tuning on examples improves results, and feedback from people can cut errors by half. The best fine tuned model reached 83.8 percent on harder math problems. However, even strong models generally could not predict what their generated code would output for a given input. For executives, this means AI coding tools can help write code but should not be trusted without review and testing. It informs decisions about where to use AI assisted development, how much human oversight to require, and what validation to build into audits.
explain_practitioner: The authors tested language models from 244 million to 137 billion parameters on two new Python benchmarks, MBPP and MathQA-Python, using few shot prompting and fine tuning. MBPP has 974 tasks while MathQA-Python has 23,914 harder text to code problems. Performance improved log linearly with model size. Their largest model reached 59.6 percent on MBPP with a carefully chosen few shot prompt and no code fine tuning. Fine tuning on a reserved dataset part added about ten points for most sizes and the largest fine tuned model reached 83.8 percent on MathQA-Python. Feedback from a person in ordinary language cut errors by half. Models generally could not predict program outputs.
